plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.

elements: upward-opening paraboloid bowl surface (cream interior left, blue right rim, orange lower flank)
vertical z-axis arrow rising through the bowl center
y-axis arrow running to the right
x-axis arrow coming forward to the lower left
short dashed axis segments near the origin (hidden portions)
black dot P0 on the near (viewer-facing) flank of the bowl
leader line and label 'P0 (x0, y0, z0)' to the right of the dot
orange arrow leaving P0 angling up-and-right along the steepest rise (surface ∇f direction)
dark blue arrow leaving P0 angling down-and-left (surface −∇f direction)
teal level curve wrapping horizontally around the bowl at P0's height
pair of teal arrows tangent to the level curve at P0 (zero-change directions)
red dashed vertical drop lines from P0 and from each arrow tip down to the plane
gray dashed drop line from the origin/axis region down to the plane
flat projection region on the plane below holding a small flattened copy of the arrows
black dot on the plane (projection of P0)
orange arrow on the plane labeled '∇f' with note 'Most rapid increase in f'
dark blue arrow on the plane labeled '−∇f' with note 'Most rapid decrease in f'
teal arrows on the plane labeled 'Zero change in f'
small right-angle square marker between the gradient direction and the level direction on the plane
rotatable unit direction arrow u at P0 (driven by the angle slider) and its dashed projection onto the plane
live numeric readout of the directional derivative D_u f

interactions.label: Direction angle θ at P0
interactions.teaches: Sweeping the direction arrow u through a full turn makes the directional derivative D_u f = |∇f|·cos θ pass from its maximum (u aligned with ∇f), through zero (u tangent to the level curve), to its minimum (u opposite ∇f), showing that alignment with the gradient alone controls the rate of change

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Flattening the three direction arrows onto the plane below exposes the right angle between the gradient and the level-curve direction, making the perpendicularity of ∇f to the zero-change direction directly visible
Hovering ∇f, −∇f, or the teal level direction highlights the matching surface arrow and its label, clarifying which direction gives maximum increase, maximum decrease, and zero change at P0

demo_steps.title: Aligned with ∇f (max increase)
demo_steps.narration: With θ=0 the direction arrow u coincides with the orange ∇f arrow; the readout shows D_u f at its positive maximum |∇f|.

demo_steps.title: Tangent to level curve (zero change)
demo_steps.narration: At θ=90° u lies along the teal level curve; the directional derivative reads 0 because u is perpendicular to the gradient.

demo_steps.title: Opposite ∇f (max decrease)
demo_steps.narration: At θ=180° u points along the blue −∇f arrow; the readout reaches its negative minimum −|∇f|, the steepest descent.

demo_steps.title: Flatten to the plane
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the plane projection drops the arrows flat; the right-angle square between ∇f and the teal level direction makes their perpendicularity explicit.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use f(x,y) = (x^2 + y^2)/4 so the surface is z = f; bowl radius ~2.5 world units, rim height ~1.56, drawn over x,y ∈ [-2.5, 2.5]. Place P0 on the near flank at roughly (x0, y0) = (1.4, -1.0) giving z0 ≈ 0.74; ∇f = (x/2, y/2) so the gradient points radially outward in the xy-plane and the level curve is the circle x^2+y^2 = x0^2+y0^2 (the teal horizontal wrap). Surface ∇f arrow = radial-outward + upward tilt; −∇f arrow = radial-inward + downward tilt; teal arrows tangent to the circle. Axes span ~±3; z-axis vertical, y-axis screen-right, x-axis screen-forward-left. The flat projection sits on a plane near z = -1.2 holding a scaled (~0.5×) flattened copy with the right-angle square between the orange and teal directions. Colors: bowl interior cream #f3ecd8, right rim blue #a9c6e6, lower flank orange #e8703a; level curve & zero-change arrows teal #1fa8a0; ∇f arrow orange #e0561a; −∇f arrow dark blue #1c3a8c; drop lines red #cc3333 (dashed) and gray #888888 (dashed); axes black. Directional derivative readout D_u f = |∇f|·cos θ with θ from the slider.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the paraboloid with a ParametricGeometry (or LatheGeometry of z=r^2/4) using a vertex-colored or two-material gradient (cream→blue across the rim, orange on the lower flank) to match the source shading. Keep both the surface-arrow group and the plane-projection group in the scene and show/hide on the viewMode toggle rather than rebuilding. The rotatable u arrow and its plane projection, plus the D_u f readout, must update reactively every slider tick; compute u in the tangent plane at P0 by rotating the in-plane gradient direction by θ. Hover highlighting should brighten the matching arrow material and bold its label. Render dashed drop lines with LineDashedMaterial and call computeLineDistances.

authoredContext:
Suppose the function z=f(x,y) is differentiable at (x0,y0) (the figure).

The ‖u‖ disappears because u is a unit vector. Therefore, the directional derivative is equal to the magnitude of the gradient evaluated at (x0,y0) multiplied by cosφ. Recall that cosφ ranges from −1 to 1. If φ=0, then cosφ=1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u both point in the same direction. If φ=π, then cosφ=−1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u point in opposite directions. In the first case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is maximized; in the second case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is minimized. If ∇f(x0,y0)=0, then Duf(x0,y0)=∇f(x0,y0)·u=0 for any vector u. These three cases are outlined in the following theorem.

The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.

An upward facing paraboloid in xyz space with point P0 (x0, y0, z0). From this point, there are arrows going up, down, and around the paraboloid. On the xy plane, the point (x0, y0) is marked, and the corresponding arrows are drawn onto the plane: the down arrow corresponds to −∇f (most rapid decrease in f), the up arrow corresponds to ∇f (most rapid increase in f), and the arrows around correspond to no change in f. The up/down arrows are perpendicular to the around arrows in their projection on the plane.

The figure shows a portion of the graph of the function f(x,y)=3+sinxsiny. Given a point (a,b) in the domain of f, the maximum value of the gradient at that point is given by ‖∇f(a,b)‖. This would equal the rate of greatest ascent if the surface represented a topographical map. If we went in the opposite direction, it would be the rate of greatest descent.
